Pass-rate delta is small (+0.06) because 3 of 5 evals (listening, writing, honesty) pass 100% in both configurations - the assertions for those evals check correctness/safety properties a strong base model already handles well, not channel-specific grounding.

The two evals with a real pass-rate gap (reading: 1.0 vs 0.857, speaking: 1.0 vs 0.857) both fail the baseline on a concrete, meaningful behavior: the baseline reading run refuses to give any band estimate at all, and the baseline speaking run buries its text-based-limitation caveat at the end instead of stating it upfront where a student would see it before running the whole test.

Across evals 2, 4, and 5, the real differentiator the skill provides is qualitative grounding (named channel frameworks like '100% Rule', 'Peacock vocabulary', 'Shopping List', and citations to specific real mock-test transcripts/video counts) rather than pass/fail - the current assertions under-test this. Several eval_feedback entries in the per-run grading.json files suggest adding assertions that check for cited source evidence or named channel concepts.

with_skill runs took noticeably longer and used more tokens on the 3 evals requiring deep domain content (reading, speaking, writing) - expected, since the skill instructs loading a ~300-430 line reference file before doing that work. For the 2 shorter evals (listening, honesty) the gap is much smaller.

Sample size is 1 run per configuration per eval (not the usual 3), so stddev/min/max within a configuration reflect across-eval variance, not run-to-run noise - these numbers should not be read as measuring consistency of a single eval.
